title: India’s Rise: From Promise to Platform for Global Growth
summary: India's growth is reshaping the global market and making it a strategic hub for technology and investment, for SAP especially. Read more.
body_markdown:
India’s emergence is not a single story of growth, but a set of connected shifts changing how global companies think about markets, talent, technology, and innovation.


India today is an industrial and technology powerhouse, and it has become a strategic center for global business, technology, innovation, and investment. For SAP, that makes India not only an important domestic market, but also a place where enterprise technology is built, tested, and scaled for global impact.


The forces behind India’s rise are structural, not cyclical: economic scale, deep technology talent, and digital infrastructure built for mass adoption. Together, they have shifted India from a market companies serve or source from into one where global technology strategy is designed, tested, and scaled.

## **A $5 trillion economy**


India’s growth, demographic scale, engineering talent, digital infrastructure, and expanding technology capabilities have set the pace for global growth and enterprise digital transformation.


India is already one of the fastest-growing major economies, with annual GDP growth of roughly 6.5% to 7% and an economy of about US$4.15 trillion today.


At its present growth rate, India is on track to cross the $5 trillion threshold shortly and become the world’s third-largest economy, overtaking Japan and Germany. By the end of the decade, India’s GDP is expected to be between $6 trillion and $7 trillion.


These are more than numerical milestones. A market of India’s size already influences global investment priorities, supply chain decisions, technology adoption, and corporate growth strategies.


Several structural advantages support this growth: a large domestic market with a population of 1.4 billion, rising affluence, and rapid urbanization that is increasing demand for infrastructure, housing, transportation, financial services, healthcare, and consumer products.


Government policy has reinforced this momentum through tax changes, foreign direct investment rules, production-linked incentives, and sustained infrastructure investment in ports, highways, logistics corridors, and renewable energy.

## **Capital investment**


At the same time, manufacturing investment has expanded as multinational companies have sought to diversify global supply chains and establish alternatives to excessive dependence on China and other production centers.


As incomes rise, consumption has expanded; as investment has increased, productivity has improved; and as productivity has improved, India has become more attractive to global capital. This feedback loop is giving the economy its own growth momentum while deepening its integration with global markets.


This shift has also changed how global executives view India. Companies that once treated India as a back-office or low-cost manufacturing base are now recalibrating it as a demand market, innovation hub, and source of global momentum.


## **A talent engine like no other**


With more than one billion citizens under 35 and more than 2.5 million STEM graduates each year, India has one of the world’s deepest reservoirs of technology talent. That talent spans engineering, computer science, data science, mathematics, and applied sciences, feeding industries such as software engineering, semiconductor design, cloud infrastructure, cybersecurity, and artificial intelligence.


India’s universities, including the world-renowned IIT network, are also evolving. The IndiaAI Mission, launched in March 2024 with a budget of about $1.1 billion, supports AI research, compute infrastructure, and skills development so India can build AI systems, not just operate them.


This talent depth changes the calculus for global employers. It allows companies to staff large engineering initiatives at a scale that is difficult to match in most markets, making India a preferred location for next-generation engineering and innovation functions.


## **A full-stack digital nation**


India’s digital transformation has provided another distinctive advantage: digital identity, payments, financial services, government platforms, and expanding connectivity built at national scale. This has created an environment where digital products can reach hundreds of millions of users quickly, giving companies a vast, real-world laboratory for new technologies and business models.


The country has long been a preferred offshore location for multinationals’ software and services work, now concentrated in Global Capability Centers. Over half of the world’s dedicated GCCs are located in India, where they employ nearly 2.1 million professionals and account for about 45% of major-city commercial office leasing.


These centers, which are expected to generate about $100 billion in export revenues this year, no longer simply provide back-office support. They have become full-stack innovation hubs running software development, product engineering, data analytics, cybersecurity operations, and AI and machine learning initiatives for their parent organizations.


Global banks like JP Morgan, technology giants including Google and Microsoft, and hundreds of others run mission-critical digital transformation programs out of India, not because it is the cheapest option, but because it has become one of the most capable.


This shift from cost arbitrage to capability arbitrage defines India’s current GCC boom. It shows that India has become a place where the world’s largest enterprises build and test their digital future, not merely maintain outsourced systems.


## **AI-ready by design**


India also has the four conditions needed to become a[leading artificial intelligence economy](https://news.sap.com/2026/11/how-india-drives-sap-ai-future/) : data at scale, developer depth, compute investment, and a favorable policy framework.


First, data volume: more than a billion people generate data across payments, e-commerce, telecommunications, and government digital services, creating a critical input for training and refining AI systems at scale.


Second, the developer ecosystem: India has one of the world’s largest software developer populations, with a growing share focused on AI and machine learning and supported by a vibrant startup environment.


A recent GitHub report found that India added more than 5.2 million developers in one year, accounting for one in three new developers on the platform worldwide and is the second-largest contributor to GitHub AI projects.


Third, investment: AI startup funding rose sharply in 2025 across large language models, enterprise tools, and sector-specific applications. The IndiaAI Datasets Platform is also building public and private datasets for developers.


Fourth, regulation: India’s policy framework for data protection and AI governance is maturing toward a model that aims to balance innovation with accountability rather than defaulting to either extreme.


## **The strategic takeaway**


Together, these factors position India not just to adopt AI built elsewhere, but to shape how AI and AI agents are built, deployed, and scaled globally. For example, India has become central to SAP’s AI strategy. Today over 80% of SAP’s AI agents are built in India, and India itself is[one of SAP’s fastest-growing markets](https://news.sap.com/?p=248685) .


India’s emergence as a global economic and technological superpower is a reality. Its economy is growing faster than peers at comparable scale, its talent base is among the world’s deepest, its digital infrastructure is proven, and its AI ecosystem is moving from adoption to innovation.


Moving forward, India’s success will depend on how effectively it converts scale into productivity, talent into innovation, and digital infrastructure into globally competitive businesses while managing social and other challenges. The foundations are in place; the next decade will show whether India’s remarkable emergence as one of the world’s largest economies and principal engines of economic and technological growth can be sustained.
